of primary CSCC could be a limitation for future analyses. Missingness was either due to not using synoptic reporting by the pathologist or the use of AJCC staging instead of BWH staging in the Netherlands. More than half of all pathology reports were synoptic reports, which were reported according to a standard protocol and thus included all important tumour characteristics for AJCC staging. In the pathology reports where synoptic reporting was not used, the pathologist did not report whether or not the high risk features were observed. Most likely the high risk feature was not present if it was not reported by the pathologist. The amount of missing data ranged from 0% to 26% for most tumor characteristics, but was higher for ‘invasion beyond subcutaneous fat’ and ‘BWH T-stage’. The reason for this is that AJCC is used in the Netherlands and one BWH high risk feature is therefore not routinely reported (i.e., invasion beyond subcutaneous fat). The other BWH risk factors are included in synoptic reports. In future analyses of data from DKCC these missing data will be taken into account properly (e.g., by applying multiple imputation methods). Not all locally advanced primary CSCC could be included in the DKCC, but the random selection assured that all subgroups of locally advanced primary CSCC were included and no selection based on treatment or tumour characteristics was made. We also included all primary tumours of patients that developed metastasis or a recurrence and it is likely that these primary tumours have the highest risk features. Therefore the distribution of the tumour characteristics among our total sample of locally advanced CSCC most likely does not reflect the distribution of these characteristics among all locally advanced CSCC in the population. This means that this distribution cannot be regarded as a population-based distribution of tumour characteristics, but as all subgroups of locally advanced primary CSCC were included by using a random selection, valid analyses can be performed in the future to investigate the association between these tumour characteristics and risk of progression. To our knowledge, the DKCC is the first real-world nationwide longitudinal data source on advanced CSCC. To decrease the burden on the healthcare system due to the high and rising incidence of CSCC, accurate prognostic models for advanced CSCC are needed to identify which patients would benefit most from specific diagnostics or treatments at different stages. Data from the DKCC will contribute to this aim and support establishing evidence-based guidelines for diagnostics, treatment, and follow-up of advanced CSCC. documents.title: Guidelines care cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Skin cancer is one of the most common malignant neoplasms in humans, and its incidence continues to rise worldwide [ , ]. It is broadly divided into melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), with NMSC mainly comprising basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Although melanoma accounts for only around 1% of skin cancers, it causes the majority of skin cancer-related deaths [ ]. Advances in early detection and treatment have improved survival, but the global burden of melanoma is expected to increase in the coming decades as a result of ageing populations and cumulative ultraviolet radiation exposure [ ]. Surgical excision remains the primary therapeutic approach for melanoma, and in early-stage disease, cure rates are generally high. However, patients with advanced melanoma and lymph node or distant organ involvement require additional interventions such as lymphadenectomy, immunotherapy or targeted therapies [ ]. The introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapies has significantly reduced melanoma mortality and transformed the prognosis of many patients with advanced or metastatic disease [ ]. Consequently, an increasing number of individuals live for many years after their initial diagnosis and treatment, transitioning into a long-term survivorship phase. SCC is the second most common skin cancer after BCC and represents the most clinically relevant keratinocyte carcinoma in terms of potential morbidity and mortality [ ]. In Spain, the estimate incidence of SCC is 38.1 cases per 100,000 person-years and with a mortality rate of 1.10 per 100,000 person-years [ ]. While many tumours follow an indolent course, SCC can grow rapidly and carries a significant risk of local recurrence and metastasis, particularly in the presence of high-risk features such as immunosuppression, increased tumour thickness or poor differentiation [ ]. Surgery is the treatment of choice for most cases and may be complemented by radiotherapy in patients with positive margins or other high-risk factors, whereas systemic immunotherapy is increasingly used in locally advanced or metastatic disease [ ]. As with melanoma, improvements in diagnosis and treatment have contributed to a growing population of SCC survivors, many of whom are older adults with multiple comorbidities and repeated interventions on chronically sun-damaged skin. Beyond oncological outcomes, the diagnosis of skin cancer can profoundly affect patients’ lives and those of their families. High survival rates mean that patients often undergo long-term follow-up, transforming skin cancer into a chronic condition that can affect patients’ lifestyles and social and professional activities. In addition to treatment, regular dermatological and oncological visits, repeated diagnostic tests and procedures, and the possibility of developing new primary tumours or metastases sustain a sense of ongoing vulnerability [ ]. Elevated levels of fear of cancer recurrence and disease progression have been associated with depression and anxiety, reduced quality of life and greater healthcare utilisation across different cancer types, including melanoma [ ]. However, psychosocial experiences are unlikely to be homogeneous across skin cancer types. Melanoma tends to affect a relatively younger population and is often perceived as a potentially lethal disease even in early stages, whereas SCC more frequently affects older patients who may already be coping with chronic illnesses, functional limitations and caregiving needs [ ]. These differences in age, comorbidities, tumour location and treatment intensity may shape how patients interpret their diagnosis, the meaning they attribute to follow-up, and the kinds of support they require. Qualitative research offers a unique avenue to explore how patients understand and live with skin cancer, complementing quantitative studies focused on symptoms, quality-of-life scores or survival. A qualitative systematic review by Bath-Hextall et al. highlighted that patients with skin cancer frequently report fear of recurrence, uncertainty about the future, body image concerns, impacts on work and social life, and unmet information needs [ ]. However, most of the available qualitative literature has either focused on melanoma or has examined skin cancer as a single entity without clearly distinguishing between melanoma and keratinocyte carcinomas [ ]. SCC remains comparatively underexplored despite its potential for aggressive behaviour, treatments that may be disfiguring or functionally impairing, and frequent occurrence in older, frail or immunosuppressed patients [ ]. Consequently, little is known about whether the emotional trajectories, fears and perceived life changes in patients with SCC differ from those of patients with melanoma, or about the specific psychosocial needs that might arise in each group. A better understanding of these aspects is essential for designing patient-centred models of care and to integrate psycho-oncological and supportive interventions into routine skin cancer management. Clarifying similarities and differences between melanoma and high-risk SCC may help clinicians tailor information, communication and follow-up strategies according to patients’ expectations, perceived risks and life circumstances rather than solely tumour biology. To address these gaps, this qualitative study investigates the emotional experiences and fears of individuals diagnosed with melanoma or high-risk SCC, examining how these evolve over time and

A better understanding of these aspects is essential for designing patient-centred models of care and to integrate psycho-oncological and supportive interventions into routine skin cancer management. Clarifying similarities and differences between melanoma and high-risk SCC may help clinicians tailor information, communication and follow-up strategies according to patients’ expectations, perceived risks and life circumstances rather than solely tumour biology. To address these gaps, this qualitative study investigates the emotional experiences and fears of individuals diagnosed with melanoma or high-risk SCC, examining how these evolve over time and influence relationships and perceived changes in everyday life. By comparing patients with melanoma and high-risk SCC, we seek to generate knowledge that can inform clinical practice guidelines and survivorship programmes for people living with skin cancer. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design This qualitative study was conducted at the Virgen de las Nieves University Hospital using semi-structured interviews with patients diagnosed with melanoma or SCC. The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist was used to guide the design and reporting of the study [ ]. 2.2. Participants Inclusion Criteria: Patients with confirmed diagnosis of melanoma for between 1 and 3 years before the inclusion, treated at the Skin Cancer Unit of the Dermatology Department of the Virgen de las Nieves University Hospital. Patients with confirmed diagnosis of SCC for between 1 and 3 years before the inclusion, treated at the Skin Cancer Unit of the Dermatology Department of the Virgen de las Nieves University Hospital. SCC cases treated in this unit are classified as high-risk SCC, categorised according to the Brigham and Women’s Hospital staging system [ ] as T2a, T2b, T3 or as having disseminated disease. Age ≥ 18 years. Ability to understand and participate in a verbal conversation. Provision of written informed consent to participate in the study. Exclusion Criteria: Physical or mental conditions that did not allow completion of an interview. Lack of written informed consent form. 2.3. Sampling Method Purposive sampling was conducted to achieve maximum diversity based on the following segmentation criteria to generate different profiles: Gender: male, female. Age (years): <65, ≥65. Tumour type: melanoma, SCC. Tumour stage: early (stage I, stage II), advanced (stage III, stage IV) [ ]. To recruit participants, patients attending the Skin Cancer Clinic of the Dermatology Department at Virgen de las Nieves University Hospital were approached after their consultation and briefly informed about the study. They were asked whether they would be willing to participate in an interview about their experiences with skin cancer. Patients who expressed interest received an information sheet and an informed consent form; for those who agreed to participate, an interview was scheduled and conducted. Recruitment was stopped once all predefined sampling groups were represented and interview data no longer generated new relevant information. 2.4. Data Collection, Variables and Sources of Information Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews conducted between June and December 2024 by two members of the research team (P.D.-C., C.U.-P.) with prior experience in clinical interviewing and training in qualitative methods. A semi-structured interview guide was specifically developed for this study after a review of the literature on the psychosocial impact of skin cancer and discussion within the Skin Cancer Unit. The guide consisted of a small number of broad, open-ended questions inviting participants to describe how they experienced being told that they had skin cancer, their main fears at that time, the people they thought about when they received the result, how their view of the disease had evolved over time and how their life had changed since the diagnosis. Additional short follow-up prompts were used when needed to clarify or deepen issues raised by participants. The initial version of the guide was discussed by the research team to ensure clinical relevance and clarity. During the first interviews, the guide was reviewed on a weekly basis and minor wording changes and reordering of questions were made to improve flow and comprehension while preserving the core content. The final version of the semi-structured interview guide is provided in . The interviews were conducted individually, face-to-face, in a quiet, private consultation room within the Dermatology Department, immediately after the clinical appointment. Only the interviewer and the participant were present, with the door closed to ensure privacy and confidentiality. Interviews lasted 20–45 min. All interviews were conducted in Spanish, audio-recorded and subsequently transcribed verbatim by the interviewer. A second researcher (S.A.-S., A.M.-L.) checked each transcript against the corresponding audio file to ensure accuracy. Finally, the transcripts were anonymised before analysis. 2.5. Statistical Analysis Participants’ socio-demographic and clinical characteristics were summarised using simple descriptive statistics (absolute frequencies and percentages). Given the qualitative design and sample size, no inferential statistical tests were performed. For the qualitative data, an inductive thematic analysis

All interviews were conducted in Spanish, audio-recorded and subsequently transcribed verbatim by the interviewer. A second researcher (S.A.-S., A.M.-L.) checked each transcript against the corresponding audio file to ensure accuracy. Finally, the transcripts were anonymised before analysis. 2.5. Statistical Analysis Participants’ socio-demographic and clinical characteristics were summarised using simple descriptive statistics (absolute frequencies and percentages). Given the qualitative design and sample size, no inferential statistical tests were performed. For the qualitative data, an inductive thematic analysis was conducted following Braun and Clarke’s approach to identify and organise patterns of meaning in the narratives of the interviews [ ]. The analysis was conducted with the assistance of NVivo 12.4 (QSR International). Two researchers (A.S.-M., J.Á.R.-P.) participated in data coding. First, they independently coded a subset of eight interviews. They then met to compare their coding, discuss differences and agree on a common list of codes and definitions, which formed a preliminary codebook. This codebook was discussed with the rest of the research team (A.M.-L., S.A.-S., P.D.-C., C.U.-P.) and refined by consensus. Using the agreed codebook, the same two researchers (A.S.-M., J.Á.R.-P.) coded all remaining interviews. New codes, necessary modifications and any ambiguous segments were discussed in regular research team meetings, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Finally, the set of codes and the thematic structure were reviewed and approved by the senior researchers (A.M.-L., S.A.-S.). No formal inter-rater agreement coefficient was calculated; instead, analytical rigour was sought through initial double coding, iterative discussion and consensus-based interpretation. 2.6. Ethical Considerations The study involved data collection from medical records and interviews, without any interventions that posed additional risks to participants. Informed consent was obtained from all participants, in accordance with current regulations on personal data protection and digital rights. Provision of written informed consent was a prerequisite for participation and was verbally reconfirmed at the beginning of each interview. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Hospital Universitario Virgen de las Nieves (protocol code CUALICP-01). 3. Results Thirty-six participants (18 with melanoma, 18 with SCC) were recruited ( ). The analysis identified three main themes: feelings, relationships and life changes. 3.1. Feelings 3.1.1. Before Diagnosis (<xref rid="jcm-14-08891-t002" ref-type="table">Table 2</xref>) Patients experienced mixed emotions upon noticing a skin lesion. Worry was common when previous knowledge or experience raised suspicion, whereas others felt tranquil, attributing lesions to non-cancerous causes. 3.1.2. At Diagnosis (<xref rid="jcm-14-08891-t003" ref-type="table">Table 3</xref>) Patients frequently reported shock upon hearing the word “cancer”. Concern about the disease’s severity and treatment followed, although some reacted with indifference or acceptance, depending on prior knowledge or previous experiences with cancer. 3.1.3. After Diagnosis (<xref rid="jcm-14-08891-t004" ref-type="table">Table 4</xref>) After diagnosis, concern about recurrence persisted for many participants, while others coped through resignation or optimism. Some SCC patients became more self-conscious about their condition, and others felt confused about needing close monitoring despite feeling completely healthy. Over time, many participants reported a gradual sense of tranquillity as they adapted to treatment and gained clarity about their disease. 3.1.4. Future Concerns (<xref rid="jcm-14-08891-t005" ref-type="table">Table 5</xref>) Many patients feared recurrence, whereas others expressed acceptance of their fate. Specific fears included death, suffering and loss of autonomy, as well as aesthetic concerns, especially after multiple interventions. 3.2. Relationships (<xref rid="jcm-14-08891-t006" ref-type="table">Table 6</xref>) 3.2.1. Family Family was perceived as a crucial source of support but also a cause of concern, as patients worried about causing distress to loved ones, particularly among women with caring responsibilities for dependent relatives. In addition, family served as a source of memories, often bringing to mind previous experiences of cancer in relatives. 3.2.2. Healthcare Professionals Patients generally expressed trust in healthcare professionals, although some described negative experiences related to communication or treatment delays. 3.3. Life Changes (<xref rid="jcm-14-08891-t007" ref-type="table">Table 7</xref>) 3.3.1. Precautions and Surveillance Following diagnosis, patients adopted precautionary measures, especially regarding sun exposure, and were vigilant about monitoring new skin lesions. 3.3.2. Working and Daily Life Many patients adjusted their working life or retired early because of the impact of the diagnosis and its treatment. Treatment side effects influenced their ability to perform daily tasks. 3.3.3. Health and Identity The diagnosis led to heightened health awareness, with constant self-checking and anxiety about new symptoms. Many patients described a shift in values and priorities as a result of their illness, and some SCC patients reported feeling different about their appearance. 4. Many patients described a shift in values and priorities as a result of their illness, and some SCC patients reported feeling different about their appearance. 4. Discussion The present study offers valuable insights into the emotional experiences, coping mechanisms and life adjustments of patients diagnosed with melanoma and SCC. By exploring patients’ nuanced reactions to diagnosis and treatment, this study highlights common psychological challenges, including worry, acceptance and the impact on relationships and daily life. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of patient experiences, which can inform tailored psychosocial support strategies and improve patient-centred care. The diagnosis of skin cancer has a significant impact on patients’ emotional, psychological and social well-being, irrespective of cancer type [ ]. However, the nature of this impact varies depending on patients’ prior concerns. Those with heightened anxiety before diagnosis often report relief afterwards, a shift they attribute to online information-seeking behaviours. While such information can alleviate immediate fears, it may also increase stress due to its generic and non-personalised nature, fostering uncertainty [ ]. Conversely, patients who were calm or indifferent before diagnosis often experience heightened stress once the diagnosis is confirmed. This highlights the importance of healthcare providers exploring patients’ emotional experiences and existing level of knowledge to effectively mitigate the psychological impact of the diagnosis. Patients with a history of cancers or other serious illnesses may perceive skin cancer as less significant, viewing it as another challenge in a life already filled with medical hardships [ ]. However, this perspective can shift if there is a family history of cancer, even if unrelated to skin cancer, as it evokes memories of negative experiences with relatives. Family dynamics also significantly shape the patient’s journey. While families are frequently viewed as sources of support, particularly in monitoring and detecting new lesions, they can also be sources of concern. Patients, particularly women who assume caregiving roles, often experience anxiety about their family responsibilities [ , ]. Conversely, patients frequently draw comfort from their families, particularly from seeing their children established and successful, which fosters a sense of acceptance and contentment. Notably, SCC patients, who are generally older, tend to display a higher level of acceptance regarding the potential for death, possibly due to a perception of having resolved life’s major tasks [ ]. Consistent with previous research, both melanoma and SCC patients encountered difficulties in understanding information provided by healthcare professionals [ , ]. When their questions remained unanswered following consultations, many patients sought information online [ ], which often failed to address their specific concerns, exacerbating their anxiety [ ]. To address this, healthcare providers must ensure that patient inquiries are thoroughly answered in a clear and personalised manner, as satisfaction with the information received is strongly correlated with improved well-being [ , ]. Interestingly, SCC is not perceived by patients as being as serious as other cancers. While it is true that the prognosis, especially for NMSC, is generally more favourable compared to other common cancers, such as colorectal or breast cancer [ , , ], this perception can lead patients to feel uncertain or confused about the need for intensive treatment or follow-up, particularly when they feel physically healthy. This paradox is more pronounced in SCC due to the lack of symptoms such as pain or bleeding, which often makes the disease seem less real to the patient [ ]. Furthermore, the perception of SCC as a minor malignancy may be perpetuated by healthcare professionals themselves. Some SCC patients reported that their physicians did not use the word “cancer” during diagnosis, contributing to a delayed recognition of the importance of their condition. This phenomenon may stem from the excellent prognosis associated with these tumours, which differs from the general public’s perception of cancer as synonymous with poor prognosis or even death [ ]. This paternalistic approach, while likely intended to alleviate immediate distress, underscores the need for healthcare professionals to provide clear, comprehensive information, even in cases of favourable prognosis [ ]. Our findings reveal a spectrum of coping strategies among both melanoma and SCC patients, ranging from proactive lifestyle changes to the maintenance of normalcy, underscoring the highly individualised nature of these strategies [ , ]. Patients exhibited increased vigilance over their skin health, consistent with previous research [ ], but this heightened awareness was often accompanied by increased anxiety and stress about potential recurrence. This finding aligns with broader literature emphasising the pervasive fear of recurrence among cancer survivors [ , ]. Additionally, it underscores the importance of having a trusted and well-informed professional to consult when they detect any suspicious lesions [ ]. Patients exhibited increased vigilance over their skin health, consistent with previous research [ ], but this heightened awareness was often accompanied by increased anxiety and stress about potential recurrence. This finding aligns with broader literature emphasising the pervasive fear of recurrence among cancer survivors [ , ]. Additionally, it underscores the importance of having a trusted and well-informed professional to consult when they detect any suspicious lesions [ ]. Fear of recurrence transcends specific cancer types [ ]. However, the experiences of patients evolve differently over time according to the type of skin cancer. Melanoma patients generally exhibit a heightened awareness of their condition from the outset and grasp its severity. As time progresses and they witness their disease remaining dormant with no new lesions emerging, initial apprehensions gradually give way to a sense of calm, though residual fears of recurrence persist. Conversely, SCC patients may experience greater anxiety over time and subsequent follow-up visits due to the chronic nature of their condition. This divergence could be attributed to the distinct biological behaviours of the two cancers. Melanoma typically presents as a solitary lesion, with fewer new lesions detected during follow-up, while SCC is often associated with the chronic development of actinic keratoses and other lesions, keeping patients in a state of ongoing vigilance [ ]. The concept of biographical disruption is well-documented in the cancer and chronic disease literature, with patients often experiencing changes in their work, daily activities and appearance, which threaten their personal identity [ ]. Many participants in our study reported significant professional changes, such as early retirement or workplace adaptations, as a result of their diagnosis. These changes not only pose economic challenges but also necessitate emotional and social adjustments, as patients navigate shifts in their professional identity. Our findings align with studies that highlight the need for workplace adaptations and psychosocial support for cancer survivors [ , , ]. Physical limitations, especially among older SCC patients, further underscore the need for comprehensive support systems that address both practical and emotional needs. Changes in appearance, particularly in SCC patients, were more pronounced, likely because SCC often affects highly visible areas such as the face [ ]. These findings underscore the multifaceted impact of skin cancer on patients’ functional independence and emphasise the need for holistic models of care [ ]. For many patients, the diagnosis of melanoma or SCC can trigger an existential re-evaluation, leading them to reassess their values, priorities and life goals. This process highlights the resilience many individuals exhibit when confronting cancer and underscores the transformative potential of adversity [ ]. Our study offers several strengths that add meaningfully to the existing literature. The use of qualitative methods allows for an in-depth exploration of patients’ experiences, providing valuable insights into the psychosocial impact of skin cancer. By including patients with both melanoma and SCC, we offer a comprehensive understanding of the challenges faced across these different cancer types, enhancing the generalisability of our findings. Additionally, by examining various facets of patients’ post-diagnosis lives, we present a holistic perspective, which can inform the development of tailored support interventions and survivorship care plans. In clinical practice, our results can be translated into concrete actions such as incorporating brief psychosocial assessments into dermatology and skin cancer clinics, explicitly addressing fear of recurrence, clarifying the meaning of “cancer” and prognosis (particularly in SCC), and involving families in education and surveillance when appropriate. Our findings also support the integration of psycho-oncology services into skin cancer care pathways and the co-design, together with patients and caregivers, of targeted interventions (for example, psycho-educational programmes, group or individual psychological support, and digital resources) tailored to high-risk skin cancer survivors. Future research should evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of such interventions in different healthcare settings, examine long-term trajectories of emotional adjustment and fear of recurrence in distinct skin cancer subgroups, and identify which patients are most likely to benefit from additional support, ideally through longitudinal and mixed-methods designs. However, our study has several limitations. The homogeneity of our sample, drawn from specific geographic regions and specialised clinics, may introduce sampling bias, limiting the generalisability of our findings. Future research should aim to include more diverse populations to capture a wider range of experiences. Additionally, the use of self-reported data may introduce recall or social desirability bias, and the cross-sectional nature of the study may not fully capture the long-term impact of a skin cancer diagnosis. Finally, the subjective interpretation inherent in thematic analysis, despite efforts to ensure methodological rigour, remains a potential source of bias. 5. However, the needs and preferences over time may differ for melanoma and SCC, as each group experiences their disease, follow-up and risk of new lesions in distinct ways. These insights into patients’ perspectives should be reflected in clinical practice guidelines and survivorship care pathways for melanoma and SCC, including recommendations on information provision, psychosocial assessment and access to psycho-oncological support.

documents.title: AAD guidelines of care for the management of atopic dermatitis topical therapies

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Canine atopic dermatitis (cAD) affects ≤ 20%–30% of dogs, presenting as a common, chronic and distressing skin condition [ ]. The pathogenesis of cAD involves complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors, resulting in epidermal barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation and cutaneous dysbiosis [ , ]. Skin barrier dysfunction is a core factor in the pathogenesis of cAD although debate continues regarding whether it is a primary defect or secondary to inflammation [ , ]. This dysfunction manifests itself through several alterations, including abnormalities in stratum corneum (SC) proteins [ , , ], skin lipid profile changes [ , , , , ] and microbiome imbalances [ , ]. Assessment of skin barrier function in dogs typically relies on indirect measurements, such as trans epidermal water loss (TEWL) and skin pH [ , , ]. TEWL is the outward diffusion of water through the skin [ ] and the noninvasive evaluation of TEWL reflects skin barrier dysfunction, although measurement in dogs can be subject to high variability dependent on ambient surroundings and body site [ , ]. Previous studies found that elevated TEWL values are linked to decreased skin barrier function in dogs with cAD [ , , ], yet there are no internationally accepted reference values for this parameter across different skin conditions. Skin pH measurement offers an alternative with lower intra‐ and interobserver variability, and higher repeatability [ , ]. Dogs with cAD typically show more alkaline skin pH [ , , ] (normal skin pH 4.84–9.95) [ ] owing to alterations in the acidic lipid mantle [ ], reduced free amino acid production [ , ] and chronic inflammation with skin dysbiosis [ ]. As homeostasis of skin pH is an integral part of preserving barrier integrity [ , ], new approaches that target skin barrier pH values may be beneficial in dogs suffering from cAD [ , ]. In human atopic dermatitis (hAD) management, stabilising the skin barrier is a priority, with emollients playing a crucial role in daily therapy [ , ]. These nonmedicated, cost‐effective formulations soften, moisturise and hydrate the skin [ , , ]. In recent years, ‘emollient plus ’ products have emerged, containing active ingredients that reduce inflammation and restore barrier lipids [ ]. Despite evident similarities between hAD and cAD [ , ], particularly regarding compromised skin barrier function that allows allergen penetration leading to inflammation and dysbiosis [ , ], the potential role of emollients in cAD remains underexplored. To the best of the authors' knowledge, five different products fitting the emollient plus concept have been studied in dogs with cAD, with benefits including increased SC lipids, decreased clinical scores and pruritus, and reduced TEWL [ , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. The results from those studies have been summarised in Table . Therefore, considering the therapeutic potential of emollient plus in cAD and the limited evidence‐based options currently available, more practical studies are needed to assess the effectiveness of these topical interventions in real‐world settings for potential routine use. Additionally, to the best of the authors' knowledge, few studies on this topic have evaluated the owner's perspective on treatment efficacy and product sensorial properties, factors that could strongly influence treatment compliance [ , , , ]. The primary objective of the present study was to evaluate the efficacy of a novel topical emollient plus formulation as a co‐adjuvant treatment for cAD. The secondary objective was to investigate whether owners of atopic dogs perceive this treatment option as useful, efficacious, appealing and practical within the treatment plan. 2 Materials and Methods 2.1 Ethics This study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Research and Teaching of the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, University of Lisbon (no. 08/2023). Participants were client‐owned and recruited in the Dermatology Service of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital of the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, University of Lisbon. Dog owners provided informed written consent to join the study and could withdraw at any time. 2.2 Study Design and Population Twenty‐seven dogs were recruited in an unblinded, proof‐of‐concept, bench‐to‐bedside clinical study. Owners of dogs of any age diagnosed with nonseasonal cAD according to published criteria [ ] were invited to participate through the Dermatology Service of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital at the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, University of Lisbon. Dogs with food allergies or other skin diseases were excluded. All canine participants must have been on a veterinary surgeon‐approved full‐spectrum ectoparasite control regimen for ≥ 8 weeks before and during the clinical trial. At the time of recruitment, all atopic dogs were clinically stable and flare‐free. Concomitant therapeutic regimens were permitted, provided that they were administered unchanged for ≥ 8 weeks before the start of the study. Bathing with products usually used by pet owners was accepted, except on the day of

All canine participants must have been on a veterinary surgeon‐approved full‐spectrum ectoparasite control regimen for ≥ 8 weeks before and during the clinical trial. At the time of recruitment, all atopic dogs were clinically stable and flare‐free. Concomitant therapeutic regimens were permitted, provided that they were administered unchanged for ≥ 8 weeks before the start of the study. Bathing with products usually used by pet owners was accepted, except on the day of evaluation. Concurrent use of allergen immunotherapy was allowed if it had been ongoing for ≥ 12 months. The introduction of any additional therapeutic treatments throughout the study was not permitted. Dogs were ineligible if presented with uncontrolled cAD (needing further systemic medication), had a parasitic infestation, clinically and cytologically diagnosable secondary infections, a concurrent non‐cAD‐related disease affecting the skin, or if they were pregnant or lactating. Throughout the study period, dogs were kept in their usual environment, had no dietary changes and received routine antiparasitic prophylaxis. 2.3 Topical Emollient <italic toggle="no">Plus</italic> Development The novel topical emollient plus was specially tailored by our team to have a supportive and repairing effect on the skin barrier while simultaneously being suitable for application through dogs' fur. The formulation contains representative ingredients used in dermatological research, selected for their documented effects on skin lipid barrier support, keratinocyte differentiation, microbial balance and anti‐inflammatory action. These include physiological lipids, botanical oils and extracts, humectants and vitamins. The exact formulation is currently proprietary, so it cannot be disclosed as a consequence of proprietary rights. 2.4 Study Protocol The study began with an initial visit (day [D]0), during which all participating dog owners received detailed instructions on the study protocol. Mandatory follow‐up consultations were scheduled 30 days after the initial consultation (D30). The treatment protocol required a once‐a‐day application, with two doses (0.17 mL each dose) applied to common areas affected by cAD, such as the concave surface of the pinna, axillae, inguinal region, abdomen, and interdigital spaces, followed by gentle massage. Clinical assessments and skin barrier parameters were recorded before and after 30 days of treatment. Pruritus severity was quantified using a validated 10 cm Visual Analog Scale (pVAS10) [ , ], and skin lesion extent and severity were assessed via the validated Canine Atopic Dermatitis Extent and Severity Index (CADESI)‐04 [ ]. Skin barrier function was evaluated using TEWL (open chamber) and pH measurements. After acclimatisation for 15 min in the testing room, TEWL and pH were measured on the inguinal and pinnae areas using the Tewameter TM 210 (Courage + Khazaka), with 10 readings collected per site and expressed in g/m [ ]/h, and the LAQUA PH220 (Delfin Technologies), with three readings taken per site (means of 10 and three readings, respectively). Additionally, on D30, owners completed an Owner Global Assessment of Treatment Efficacy (OGATE) questionnaire [ ] and an original questionnaire pertaining to the emollient's sensorial properties, which consisted of six statements that they had to classify on a scale from 1 to 10 (1 = entirely disagree and 10 = entirely agree). The study design is schematically represented in Figure . 2.5 Exclusion Criteria Criteria for study withdrawal included adverse reactions to the emollient, worsening of clinical signs that required a change of therapy, and failure of the owner to comply with the treatment protocol and/or scheduled clinical appointments. 2.6 Statistical Methods Statistical analyses were conducted using the automated software IBM spss statistics v27.0 (IBM Corp.). A repeated‐measures ANOVA was used to assess differences in the means of the CADESI‐04, PVAS10, TEWL and skin pH variables across the two time points (D0 and D30). Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, and sphericity was evaluated using Mauchly's test. In cases where the assumption of sphericity was violated, a Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied to adjust the degrees of freedom. The statistical significance was set at a p ‐value of < 0.05. 3 Results 3.1 Sample Characterisation A total of 27 privately owned dogs with controlled, spontaneous, nonseasonal cAD were recruited. Six dogs were excluded from the study: one owing to an acute flare, one owing to loss of follow‐up, two owing to mild potential adverse effects and two dogs owing to lack of owner compliance. The remaining 21 dogs completed the clinical trial and were included in the statistical analysis. Among these, 13 were males (61.90%) and eight were females (38.10%). Regarding the reproductive status, nine were intact (42.86%) and 12 were neutered (57.14%). The mean age was 4.97 ± 2.88 years (range 1–11 years). Breeds included French bulldog ( n = 4, 19.05%), Labrador retriever ( n = 3, 14.29%), mixed‐breed ( n = 3, 14.29%), West Highland white terrier ( n =

A repeated‐measures ANOVA revealed a significant decrease in the mean pVAS10 values from D0 to D30 (D0 = 4.25 ± 1.85; D30 = 3.38 ± 1.79; p = 0.016). The evolution of a visual pruritus score throughout the 30‐day period of emollient application is represented in Figure . Of the 21 dogs, 17 (80.95%) showed an improvement in pruritus scores after 30 days, with an average decrease of 27% among responders. Four (19.05%) did not improve, and two (9.52%) experienced an increase in the pVAS10 severity classification. Initially, 14 dogs (66.67%) had moderate‐to‐severe pVAS10 scores, three (14.29%) had mild cAD scores and four (19.05%) had normal pVAS10 values (< 2). After treatment, only six dogs (28.57%) remained in the moderate‐to‐severe category, while 10 (47.62%) were classified as mild and five (23.81%) achieved normal status (Figure ). 3.3 Extent and Severity of Skin Lesions Recorded CADESI‐04 scores for each dog at both time points are presented in Table . A repeated‐measures ANOVA revealed a significant decrease in the mean CADESI‐04 values from D0 to D30 (D0 = 24.62 ± 18.48; D30 = 13.43 ± 7.44; p = 0.02). The evolution of the CADESI‐04 scores throughout the 30‐day period of emollient application is represented in Figure . Improvement was observed in 16 dogs (76.19%), with an average decrease of 47% among responders. Four (19.05%) did not improve and one (4.76%) experienced an increase in severity classification. At baseline, six dogs (28.57%) had moderate‐to‐severe CADESI‐04 scores, 13 (61.90%) had mild scores and two (9.52%) had normal CADESI‐04 values (< 10). Post‐treatment, no dogs remained in the severe category; only one (4.76%) was classified as moderate, 14 (66.67%) were classified as mild and six (28.57%) achieved a normal status (Figure ). A significant interaction was found between initial CADESI‐04 severity and improvement over time ( p < 0.001), indicating that dogs with more severe initial lesions showed greater improvement (Figure ). 3.4 Skin Barrier Indirect Parameters The mean TEWL value in the inguinal region was 13.62 ± 14.59 g/m 2 /h on D0 (range 1.14–58.73 g/m 2 /h). By D30, the mean TEWL had increased to 15.32 ± 15.17 g/m 2 /h (range 1.47–59.98 g/m 2 /h). Regarding the pinnae, the mean TEWL value on D0 was 18.63 ± 17.33 g/m 2 /h (range 3.20–75.34 g/m 2 /h). By D30, this value had decreased to 9.56 ± 10.75 g/m 2 /h (range 0.92–44.46 g/m 2 /h). A repeated‐measures ANOVA confirmed that the reduction in TEWL in the pinnae was statistically significant ( p = 0.049), while the increase observed in the inguinal region was not ( p = 0.75). The mean pH value in the inguinal region was 6.33 ± 1.24 on D0 (range 3.97–9.36). By D30, the mean pH value had decreased slightly to 6.12 ± 1.13 (range 3.43–8.84). In the pinnae, the mean pH value on D0 was 6.07 ± 0.97 (range 4.33–8.38), decreasing to 5.41 ± 0.71 (range 3.86–5.32) on D30. ANOVA confirmed that the reduction in pH in the pinnae was statistically significant ( p = 0.01), while the decrease in the inguinal region was not ( p = 0.54). The variations in TEWL and pH across both anatomical sites are represented in Figure . 3.5 Owners' Overall Assessment of the Therapeutic Efficacy After 30 days of daily emollient plus application, 19 owners (90.47%) rated the treatment response as ‘good’ or ‘excellent’ (OGATE ≥ 3). One owner (4.76%) rated the response as ‘fair’ (OGATE = 2) and one (4.76%) rated it as ‘poor’ (OGATE = 1). 3.6 Sensorial Scores The statements used to evaluate the product (rated 1–10; 1—disagree entirely and 10 + agree entirely) are represented in Figure , along with the mean scores for each statement. The sensorial evaluation revealed exceptionally high owner satisfaction with the emollient plus formulation. One owner (4.76%) rated the response as ‘fair’ (OGATE = 2) and one (4.76%) rated it as ‘poor’ (OGATE = 1). 3.6 Sensorial Scores The statements used to evaluate the product (rated 1–10; 1—disagree entirely and 10 + agree entirely) are represented in Figure , along with the mean scores for each statement. The sensorial evaluation revealed exceptionally high owner satisfaction with the emollient plus formulation. Owners rated the product highly across all categories, with mean scores ranging from 8.39 to 9.39 of 10, particularly appreciating its good appearance (9.39 ± 1.2) and pleasant smell (9.29 ± 1.2). Notably, owners indicated a strong willingness to include this product in their dogs' treatment plans (9.19 ± 1.1), suggesting excellent acceptability that could positively influence treatment compliance. The mean scores for the sensorial evaluation are compiled in Figure . 3.7 Reported Adverse Effects Potential adverse effects were observed in two of 27 dogs (7.40%), both Jack Russell terriers. One dog developed hyperpigmented macules (owner‐reported) in the treated areas, although this could not be clinically verified owing to loss of follow‐up. The other is likely to have experienced contact allergic dermatitis, with a mild erythematous rash in the inguinal region after 2 weeks of application. The rash disappeared after stopping the treatment and recurred upon re‐exposure, resulting in the dog's exclusion from the study. According to the owners, the hyperpigmented lesion was neither pruritic nor painful, while the erythematous lesion was mildly pruritic. When asked for the timing of onset, the first owner was specific, while the second estimated that it occurred within a few days. 4 Discussion and Conclusion The present proof‐of‐concept study is the first clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of this novel topical emollient plus formulation as an adjuvant in the treatment of cAD. To the best of our knowledge, this also was the first study in veterinary medicine that considered the owner's sensorial evaluation of a topical emollient concurrently with traditionally assessed clinical outcomes. The clinical evaluation of topical emollient formulations for dogs remains limited, with only five products studied to date (Table ). To contribute to this emerging field, a novel topical emollient plus , specifically designed for atopic dogs, incorporating evidence‐based active ingredients, was developed. The significant reduction in both pVAS10 and CADESI‐04 scores suggests that the topical emollient plus effectively addresses two fundamental clinical manifestations of cAD. The pVAS10 mean score significantly decreased from 4.25 ± 1.85 to 3.38 ± 1.75 ( p = 0.016). 17 dogs (80.95%) improved their pVAS10 scores, with a mean reduction of 27%. At D0, only 33.34% of dogs had ‘normal’ or ‘mild’ pruritus, which increased to 71.43% by D30. These results are consistent with previous literature showing significant improvement in pruritus in atopic dogs after treatment with topical emollients [ , , , ]. The mean CADESI‐04 score significantly decreased from 24.62 ± 18.48 to 13.43 ± 7.44 ( p = 0.02). Sixteen dogs (76.19%) improved their CADESI‐04 scores, representing a mean 47.70% reduction. Likewise, the proportion of dogs with ‘moderate’ or ‘severe’ skin lesions decreased from 28.57% at baseline to just 4.76% by study completion, representing a sixfold reduction. These results highlight the potential effectiveness of this emollient in managing the dermatological manifestations of cAD. As the only change in the treatment protocol for each individual was the addition of this product, the improvement in clinical outcomes may be a consequence of using this emollient plus for 30 days. This may be attributed to both direct and indirect mechanisms. The formulation contains active ingredients known for their documented direct anti‐pruritic and anti‐inflammatory properties. Indirectly, topical emollients have been shown to increase stratum corneum (SC) lipid production and organisation [ , , ], thereby restoring skin barrier function. This restoration reduces allergen penetration and increases SC hydration, lessening both pruritus and inflammation [ ]. Interestingly, dogs with higher initial CADESI‐04 scores showed greater reduction in scores throughout the study compared to those with milder initial clinical signs (Figure ). This suggests that the emollient plus may be particularly beneficial for dogs with more severe skin lesions, where the potential for improvement is greater. The observed improvements also indicate that this emollient can be a valuable adjunct therapy when used alongside established pharmacological treatments, providing additional relief of clinical signs. However, not all dogs showed improvement in clinical parameters. Four dogs experienced increased pVAS10 scores (19.05%) and five showed increased CADESI‐04 scores (23.81%). Several factors may explain these variable responses, including individual variability in response to treatment [ ], potential compliance issues and natural fluctuations in environmental allergens. Additionally, the optimal frequency for topical emollient application has not been established [ ], so some dogs may require more frequent or prolonged application regimens before seeing

observed improvements also indicate that this emollient can be a valuable adjunct therapy when used alongside established pharmacological treatments, providing additional relief of clinical signs. However, not all dogs showed improvement in clinical parameters. Four dogs experienced increased pVAS10 scores (19.05%) and five showed increased CADESI‐04 scores (23.81%). Several factors may explain these variable responses, including individual variability in response to treatment [ ], potential compliance issues and natural fluctuations in environmental allergens. Additionally, the optimal frequency for topical emollient application has not been established [ ], so some dogs may require more frequent or prolonged application regimens before seeing results. TEWL measurements showed different results between anatomical locations. In the pinnae, mean TEWL decreased significantly from 18.63 ± 17.33 to 9.56 ± 10.75 g/m 2 /h ( p = 0.049), suggesting improved skin barrier function, a finding consistent with previous literature [ , , ]. This reduction may be attributed to the capacity of the emollient to replenish the SC lipid matrix [ , , ], stimulate endogenous lipid production (nondisclosed ingredients), and enhance the skin's water‐holding capacity through its humectant and occlusive components [ ]. Conversely, TEWL values in the inguinal region showed a nonsignificant increase from 13.62 ± 14.59 to 15.32 ± 15.17 g/m 2 /h ( p = 0.75). This regional difference is consistent with previous literature [ , , , ] and may be explained by several factors. First, the inguinal region is likely to be more occluded, having higher humidity levels, and experiencing greater friction. This may contribute to higher levels of skin barrier dysfunction, which might require longer treatment periods to show improvement. Second, the inguinal SC is slightly thicker, which may limit the penetration of active ingredients [ ]. Another plausible factor is that the inguinal region may have greater exposure to household cleaning products, which are known to disrupt the skin barrier function, even in small quantities [ ]. TEWL measurements in the inguinal region also are technically more challenging as a consequence of the anatomy of the area and hair density, especially considering that an open‐chamber device was used [ , ]. Finally, although TEWL is currently considered the gold standard measurement for skin barrier assessment, its several intrinsic limitations may cause significant variation in values [ , , ]. It is worth noting that mean TEWL values obtained in this study generally aligned with those reported in the literature, with D30 pinna values approaching those typically seen in healthy dogs. Still, the existing literature mostly reports mean TEWL values and not the full ranges of TEWL measurement, which limits direct comparison with the minimum and maximum values obtained in this study. However, the considerable overlap between reported TEWL values for healthy and atopic dogs suggests that TEWL alone may have limitations as a stand‐alone assessment of skin barrier function (to see the studies, see Appendix ). Recent literature suggests that pH may be a more reliable indicator of skin barrier function owing to its lower variability [ ]. The physiological pH of a dog's skin is reported to range from 4.84 to 9.95, affected by several factors [ ]. Although reports are limited, the literature has shown that atopic dogs tend to have slightly more alkaline pH values when compared to healthy dogs [ , , ]. This study found a statistically significant decrease in pinnae pH from 6.07 ± 0.97 at baseline to 5.41 ± 0.71 after 30 days of treatment ( p = 0.01). The inguinal region also showed a reduction in pH from 6.33 ± 1.24 to 6.12 ± 1.13, although this was not statistically significant. This pH reduction is consistent with the expected outcome of using emollients in humans [ , ], which often include pH‐adjusting ingredients aimed at restoring a more balanced skin environment. Still, the mean pH value of enrolled dogs at baseline was within the reported range for healthy dogs. This may be because dogs were already undergoing treatment for cAD which could have already improved pH values. Still, while technically more reliable, skin pH measurement presents clinical limitations. The high biological individual variability can be influenced by external factors [ , ], the overlap in values from healthy and atopic skin found in previous studies, along with the absence of well‐defined, mutually exclusive ranges, complicate its clinical utility in research studies (Appendix ). Although the reduction in TEWL and pH in the pinna is promising, it is essential to investigate whether this effect can be replicated consistently across other anatomical sites and in different severities of cAD, as well as to determine the ideal application frequencies of the product for various body regions. The OGATE questionnaire revealed high owner satisfaction, with 90.47% rating the emollient as having a ‘good’ or ‘excellent’ effect on their dogs' skin condition. This positive perception is

found in previous studies, along with the absence of well‐defined, mutually exclusive ranges, complicate its clinical utility in research studies (Appendix ). Although the reduction in TEWL and pH in the pinna is promising, it is essential to investigate whether this effect can be replicated consistently across other anatomical sites and in different severities of cAD, as well as to determine the ideal application frequencies of the product for various body regions. The OGATE questionnaire revealed high owner satisfaction, with 90.47% rating the emollient as having a ‘good’ or ‘excellent’ effect on their dogs' skin condition. This positive perception is crucial in the management of cAD, where owner compliance directly impacts treatment success [ ]. The strong correlation between owner‐perceived effectiveness and measured clinical improvements suggests that the benefits of the emollient were apparent to pet owners. However, two cases where owners reported either ‘fair’ or ‘poor’ responses highlight the importance of managing expectations. In one instance, a dog showed improvements in CADESI‐04 (16 to 10), TEWL (9.05 to 7.24, mean of both locations) and pH values (7.92 to 5.92, mean of both locations), yet the owner classified the treatment efficacy as ‘poor’, indicating a discrepancy between clinical improvement and owner perception. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to report owner feedback on the sensorial properties of a topical formulation. Owners consistently rated the product highly across all sensorial properties (Figure ). The scores related to the product's sensorial properties, such as its smell and appearance, reflect its positive perception among owners. The product was also well tolerated by the dogs, indicating minimal discomfort or irritation. These high ratings suggest that the emollient is practical and pleasant to use, which could improve adherence to treatment. This is relevant as maintaining compliance with topical treatments is often challenging in veterinary dermatology [ , ]. Only two of 27 dogs (7.40%) experienced adverse effects during the trial, suggesting that the novel formulation is generally well tolerated. One case involved skin hyperpigmentation yet follow‐up was lost, limiting further assessment. The second case presented as contact dermatitis in the inguinal region, which resolved after discontinuation of the product and brief topical corticosteroid therapy after study exclusion. The occurrence of contact dermatitis aligns with existing literature on topical emollient use in atopic dogs [ ]. Besides the ones already mentioned, further limitations must be acknowledged when interpreting these findings. First, the small study size limits the generalisation of results to broader populations. Second, the absence of a control group means that improvements cannot be definitively attributed to the topical emollient alone. Future randomised, double‐blinded, placebo‐controlled trials would strengthen the evidence for efficacy. Third, owner‐administered treatments introduce potential inconsistencies in application frequency, quantity and technique, despite our efforts to standardise these factors through demonstrations and rehearsals. Finally, uncontrolled factors such as weather conditions during different recruitment periods, operator differences and patients' movement may have influenced TEWL and pH readings, affecting data interpretation. Despite the promising results, this study has found several areas requiring further research. The efficacy of the emollient plus should be tested in more diverse populations across different breeds, age groups and disease severities. Also, the exact mechanisms by which the emollient exerts its therapeutic effects remain to be fully understood. Future studies should explore these mechanisms in more detail. While improvements in TEWL and pH were significant in the pinnae, these effects were not consistent with changes in the inguinal skin. Therefore, future research must explore whether region‐specific treatment protocols could optimise the therapeutic benefits across different body areas. Besides, more sophisticated assessments may be pursued in future research, including parameters such as electrical impedance spectroscopy [ ]. This proof‐of‐concept study suggests that this topical emollient plus formulation is a safe, sensory‐pleasing and clinically effective adjuvant therapy for managing cAD. The high owner satisfaction and favourable safety profile further support its potential value in clinical practice. These preliminary findings warrant larger controlled studies to confirm efficacy and elucidate optimal treatment protocols. <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">Author Contributions</styled-content> Beatriz Fernandes: conceptualisation, methodology, investigation, formal analysis, visualisation, writing – original draft, funding acquisition. documents.title: AAD guidelines of care for the management of atopic dermatitis phototherapy and systemic therapies

chunks.content: Key Summary Points Introduction As a result of the heterogeneous nature of atopic dermatitis (AD), diverse treatment options are needed to achieve disease control [ ]. Current treatment guidelines recommend phototherapy and systemic therapies, including biologics, in patients with moderate-to-severe disease [ ]. Lebrikizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds with high affinity and slow dissociation rate to interleukin-13 (IL-13), thereby blocking the downstream signaling of IL-13 with high potency [ ]. Lebrikizumab demonstrated efficacy and a positive benefit-risk profile for the treatment of moderate-to-severe AD in adults and adolescents in previous phase 2 and 3 clinical trials, and was approved in the USA, Europe, and seven other countries worldwide for the treatment of moderate-to-severe AD in adults and adolescents [ – ]. Dupilumab, a biologic commonly used for treating moderate-to-severe AD, targets the IL-4Rɑ subunit, thereby inhibiting signaling of IL-4 and IL-13 [ – ]. Dupilumab may not be effective in all patients, and therapy is discontinued for various reasons [ ]. In real-world settings, approximately 18–20% of patients with moderate-to-severe AD discontinue dupilumab within 3–4 years of treatment, and the primary reasons reported in this group of patients are loss of effectiveness (26–40%), adverse events (AEs; 20%), and cost/insurance issues (18%) [ , ]. These discontinuations indicate a need for additional therapeutic options [ , – ]. Lebrikizumab is indicated in patients with moderate-to-severe AD that is not adequately controlled with topical prescription therapies or when those therapies are not advisable. Because lebrikizumab and dupilumab have different mechanisms of action in the treatment of AD, lebrikizumab is a potential treatment candidate for patients with moderate-to-severe AD who discontinue dupilumab. ADapt is the first study designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of lebrikizumab in reducing signs and symptoms of AD in patients with moderate-to-severe AD and with prior dupilumab experience. Here we present results from ADapt through 24 weeks of treatment with lebrikizumab. Methods Study Design ADapt was an open-label, 24-week, phase 3b study in the USA (Fig. ). Eligible patients included adolescents (aged ≥ 12 to < 18 years, weighing ≥ 40 kg) and adults who stopped dupilumab treatment for one of three reasons: (1) inadequate response (partial response, 25–50% at peak response for itch and skin; non-response, < 25% at peak response for itch and skin; or loss of response for itch and skin after treatment with dupilumab for at least 4 months at a labeled dose [Table ]); (2) AEs or intolerance, with no required prior length of dupilumab treatment (only the primary AE leading to discontinuation of dupilumab was recorded; other AEs experienced while on dupilumab were not recorded to avoid recall bias); or (3) other reasons (e.g., inability to afford treatment, health insurance changes, previous open-label clinical trial participation that completed with no discontinuation for AEs) with no required prior length of dupilumab treatment. Eligible patients were required to have moderate-to-severe AD, which was defined as baseline Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) [ ] of at least 16 (scale of 0 to 72), baseline Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) [ ] score of at least 3 (scale of 0 to 4), a baseline body surface area of at least 10%, and a history of inadequate response to treatment with topical medications. A washout period was required 2 weeks prior to baseline for topical therapy and 4 weeks prior to baseline for dupilumab and other conventional systemic drugs. Patients were excluded from the study if they were previously treated with tralokinumab. Full eligibility criteria are detailed in the Supplemental Methods. Patients received a 500 mg subcutaneous (SC) loading dose of lebrikizumab at baseline and week 2, followed by lebrikizumab 250 mg SC every 2 weeks (Q2W) until week 16. Responders at week 16, defined as achieving an IGA score of 0 or 1 with ≥ 2-point reduction from baseline (IGA 0/1) or ≥ 75% reduction in EASI from baseline (EASI 75), received lebrikizumab 250 mg SC every 4 weeks (Q4W) through week 24. Inadequate responders at week 16 continued to receive lebrikizumab 250 mg SC Q2W. Use of low- and/or mid-potency topical corticosteroids (TCSs), high-potency TCSs up to 10 consecutive days, topical calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus), and/or topical phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitors (crisaborole) was permitted as needed. Any use of topical Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, phototherapy, or systemic medications or use of high-potency TCSs for more than 10 consecutive days was considered rescue therapy and required discontinuation from the study. Ethical Approval The study was undertaken in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki [ ] and approved by the institutional review board Advarra (6100 Merriweather Drive Suite 600, Columbia, MD 21044, IRB number Pro00066943) before the study was initiated. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients before enrollment in the study. For patients considered to be minors, written consent

permitted as needed. Any use of topical Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, phototherapy, or systemic medications or use of high-potency TCSs for more than 10 consecutive days was considered rescue therapy and required discontinuation from the study. Ethical Approval The study was undertaken in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki [ ] and approved by the institutional review board Advarra (6100 Merriweather Drive Suite 600, Columbia, MD 21044, IRB number Pro00066943) before the study was initiated. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients before enrollment in the study. For patients considered to be minors, written consent of a parent or legal guardian and assent of the minor were obtained. The authors affirm that human research participants provided written informed consent for publication of all images in this article. Efficacy and Safety Outcomes A detailed description of the efficacy outcomes is provided in Table . The primary efficacy endpoint was the EASI 75 response rate at week 16. Secondary and exploratory efficacy endpoints at weeks 16 and 24 included the EASI 75 response rate at week 24; percentage improvement from baseline in EASI; percentage of patients achieving ≥ 90% reduction from baseline in EASI (EASI 90); percentage of patients achieving IGA 0/1 with ≥ 2-point improvement from baseline; percentage of patients with baseline Pruritus Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) [ ] score ≥ 4 achieving ≥ 4-point improvement from baseline; percentage of patients with baseline Sleep-Loss Scale [ ] score ≥ 2 achieving ≥ 2-point improvement from baseline; percentage of patients with baseline Skin Pain NRS [ ] score ≥ 4 achieving ≥ 4-point improvement from baseline; percentage of patients ≥ 16 years of age with baseline Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) [ ] ≥ 4 achieving ≥ 4-point improvement from baseline; percentage improvement from baseline in the Atopic Dermatitis Control Tool (ADCT) [ ]; percentage improvement from baseline in SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) score [ ]; percentage of patients achieving Face IGA (F-IGA) score of 0 or 1 with ≥ 2-point improvement from baseline (F-IGA 0/1); percentage improvement from baseline in modified Total Lesion Symptom Score (mTLSS) [ ]; and distribution of responses for Participant-Reported Satisfaction Question. Patient IGA and EASI scores were assessed at each on-site visit. Pruritus NRS, Sleep-Loss Scale, and Skin Pain NRS assessments were recorded daily by the patient using an electronic diary and are reported as prorated weekly mean scores. Safety was assessed by monitoring AEs, performing physical examinations and clinical safety laboratory tests (including hematology and chemistry), and monitoring vital signs. AEs of special interest included conjunctivitis, herpes viral infections, and parasitic infections. Statistical Analysis All efficacy analyses were based on the intent-to-treat population, defined as all enrolled patients according to their planned intervention. Data were analyzed both as observed and with imputation after combining data from the Q2W and Q4W arms after week 16 to reflect the recommended dosing regimen per US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label guidance. The imputed analyses were post hoc; patients who discontinued treatment due to lack of efficacy were imputed as non-responders, and all remaining missing data were imputed using multiple imputation. EASI 75 at week 16 was also reported after imputing missing data using last observation carried forward as a supplemental analysis. Categorical data were summarized using frequencies and percentages, and continuous data were summarized using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation. EASI 75 response rates at week 16 (primary endpoint) and week 24 were computed for the overall population and after stratifying by reasons for dupilumab discontinuation (inadequate responders, AE/intolerance, and other reasons). Where applicable, efficacy data collected at an early termination visit were mapped to the next scheduled visit. All safety data were descriptively summarized using the safety population, defined as all enrolled patients who received at least one dose of lebrikizumab 250 mg over the 24-week treatment period. Treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) were defined as AEs that first occurred or worsened in severity after the first dose of study treatment. All TEAEs reported by at least one patient were summarized using preferred terms by system organ class (Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities [MedDRA] version 25.1). Results Patient Characteristics A total of 86 patients were enrolled into the study (Table ; Fig. ). Enrollment ended early after an internal assessment determined that the study objectives could be achieved with a smaller sample size and enrollment of additional patients was unlikely to impact study conclusions. Primary reasons for prior dupilumab discontinuation were as follows: inadequate response, 48 patients (no response, n = 5; partial response, n = 32; lost response, n = 11); AEs/intolerance, 14 patients; and other reasons, 24 patients (Table ). The mean age of AD onset for the full patient population was 26.6 years and 22.3, 27.4, and 34.7 years for patients who discontinued dupilumab due to inadequate response,

Primary reasons for prior dupilumab discontinuation were as follows: inadequate response, 48 patients (no response, n = 5; partial response, n = 32; lost response, n = 11); AEs/intolerance, 14 patients; and other reasons, 24 patients (Table ). The mean age of AD onset for the full patient population was 26.6 years and 22.3, 27.4, and 34.7 years for patients who discontinued dupilumab due to inadequate response, AEs/intolerance, and other reasons, respectively. Twenty-one patients (24.4%) had severe AD (IGA score of 4) and 65 patients (75.6%) had moderate AD (IGA score of 3) at baseline. Of the 86 patients, 50 (58.1%) used only dupilumab as a prior systemic treatment, and more than 40% used at least two systemic treatments previously (including phototherapy; traditional systemic therapies such as methotrexate, cyclosporine, and systemic corticosteroids; and advanced systemic therapies such as oral JAK inhibitors). Median time between stopping dupilumab and starting lebrikizumab was 185 days. Clinical manifestations of AD reported ongoing at the time of study entry included hand dermatitis ( n = 39, 45.3%), facial dermatitis ( n = 44, 51.8%), and conjunctivitis ( n = 2, 2.3%); nonatopic comorbidities included alopecia areata ( n = 2, 2.3%); and atopic comorbidities included asthma ( n = 25, 29.1%), food allergy ( n = 16, 18.6%), and allergic rhinitis ( n = 31, 36.0%). Twenty-seven patients (31.4%) discontinued at or prior to week 16, with an additional seven discontinuing between weeks 16 and 24 (total n = 34, 39.5%). Reasons for study discontinuation included AEs ( n = 5), protocol deviation ( n = 6), lack of efficacy ( n = 1), withdrawal by subject ( n = 13), lost to follow-up ( n = 5), physician decision ( n = 2), and other reasons ( n = 2; Fig. ). EASI scores improved in most patients who discontinued due to “withdrawal by subject” and “lost to follow-up” at the time of discontinuation compared to baseline. Primary, Secondary, and Exploratory Efficacy Outcomes The EASI 75 response rate was 57.4% (35/61) at week 16 (primary endpoint) and 60.0% (33/55) at week 24 (Fig. a). At week 16, EASI 75 response rates stratified by reason for prior dupilumab discontinuation were 45.7% (16/35), 80.0% (8/10), and 68.8% (11/16) for patients who discontinued dupilumab due to inadequate response, AE/intolerance, and other reasons, respectively (Table ). Among the 35 dupilumab inadequate responders, EASI 75 response rates at week 16 were 66.7% (2/3), 33.3% (7/21), and 63.3% (7/11) for those who discontinued dupilumab due to no response, partial response, and loss of response, respectively. At week 24, EASI 75 response rates stratified by reason for prior dupilumab discontinuation were 50.0% (15/30), 77.8% (7/9), and 68.8% (11/16) for patients who discontinued dupilumab due to inadequate response, AE/intolerance, and other reasons, respectively (Table ). Among patients who discontinued dupilumab due to no response, partial response, and loss of response, 33.3% (1/3), 47.1% (8/17), and 60.0% (6/10), respectively, achieved EASI 75 at week 24 with lebrikizumab treatment. On average, the EASI improved from baseline by 73.3% at week 16 and by 77.2% at week 24 (Table ). The EASI 90 response rate was 29.1% at week 24 (Table ). Sixty-nine patients had a baseline F-IGA of at least 2 points. Of these patients, 52.3% achieved clear or almost clear skin in facial AD (F-IGA 0/1 with ≥ 2-point improvement) at week 24, with 18.8% of patients achieving F-IGA 0/1 as early as week 2 (Fig. b). Of the two patients who previously discontinued dupilumab due to facial erythema, one had completely clear facial skin (F-IGA 0) at weeks 16 and 24; data were unavailable for the other patient. mTLSS improved from baseline by an average of 68.3% at week 24 (Table ; Fig. a, b). In a post hoc analysis of the 41 patients with moderate-to-severe hand dermatitis at baseline, defined by mTLSS ≥ 12, mTLSS improved from baseline by an average of 10.9 (75.0%) at week 24. Among these patients, 29.2% achieved total clearance (mTLSS 0) for hand dermatitis at week 24 (Table ; Fig. c–e). A ≥ 4-point improvement from baseline in Pruritus NRS score, a clinically meaningful response, was reported as early as week 12 in most patients, with response rates rising over time (week 16, 53.2%, number of patients with non-missing values [Nx] = 47; week 24, 61.5%, Nx = 39 Fig. c). At week 16, response rates for ≥ 4-point improvement in Pruritus NRS score from baseline were 50.0% (11/22), 60.0% (6/10), and 53.3% (8/15) for patients who discontinued dupilumab due to inadequate response, AE/intolerance, and other reasons, respectively (Table ). Results from other secondary and exploratory outcomes are shown in Table . The proportion of patients achieving IGA 0/1 was 38.2% at week 24 (Fig. d). At least a 2-point improvement from baseline in Sleep-Loss Scale score was reported by 42.1% (8/19) of patients at week 24. At least a 4-point improvement from baseline in Skin Pain NRS score and DLQI were reported by 75.0% (21/28) and 83.0% (39/47) of patients, respectively, at week 24. Patient-reported disease control also improved after 24 weeks of lebrikizumab treatment, as measured by mean percentage improvements from baseline in ADCT (51.0%, Nx = 55). Similarly, patient- and investigator-reported disease signs and symptoms showed improvement, as measured by mean percentage improvement from baseline in SCORAD (56.4%, Nx = 54). Most patients (69.1%, Nx = 55) reported being mostly or completely satisfied with lebrikizumab as treatment for their skin condition after 24 weeks of treatment (Table ). Results for the imputed analyses were similar to the as observed results and are presented in Table . Patient improvement can also be viewed from patient photos in Fig. . EASI 75 response was similar for week 16 (87.5%) and week 24 (71.8%) in responders; 31.3% of non-responders achieved EASI 75 at week 24. IGA 0/1 response was similar for week 16 (58.5%) and week 24 (48.7%) for responders; 12.5% of non-responders achieved IGA 0/1 at week 24. The proportion of patients with ≥ 4-point improvement on the Pruritus NRS was similar at week 16 and week 24 for responders (58.6%, 65.4%, respectively) and non-responders (57.1%, 53.8%, respectively). Use of Concomitant and Rescue Medication Over the course of 24 weeks of lebrikizumab treatment, 39 of 86 patients (45.3%) used a low-to-moderate potency TCS, as permitted. Twelve of 86 patients (14.0%) used rescue medication and were discontinued, including 2 patients who used high-potency TCSs for over 10 consecutive days, one who used topical ruxolitinib, and 9 who used a prohibited systemic therapy (methylprednisolone, n = 1; prednisone, n = 5; triamcinolone acetonide, n = 1; deucravacitinib, n = 1; upadacitinib, n = 1). Details of concomitant therapies used to treat AD can be found in Table . Safety Assessments During the 24-week treatment period, TEAEs were reported by 46 patients (53.5%), and most were mild or moderate in severity (Table ). Serious AEs were reported by 2 patients (2.3%; cerebral vascular occlusion, unrelated to study treatment, and resolved; and rash morbilliform, related to study treatment, and resolved), and 5 patients (5.8%) discontinued due to an AE (dermatitis atopic, drug eruption, immune-mediated dermatitis, rash morbilliform, and headache; Table ). Conjunctivitis was reported by 3 patients (3.5%; 2 mild, 1 moderate) but did not lead to discontinuation in any patient, and none of the patients had previously stopped dupilumab due to conjunctivitis. Eye irritation ( n = 1), eye pruritus ( n = 1), arthralgia ( n = 1), and joint swelling ( n = 1) were reported by one patient each. No TEAEs of facial dermatitis or asthma were reported. Of the 14 patients with prior dupilumab discontinuation due to AEs/intolerance, 2 discontinued treatment with lebrikizumab due to an AE, including 1 with dermatitis atopic and 1 with immune-mediated dermatitis. Of note, among the 10 patients who reported eye-related events, facial dermatitis, or inflammatory arthritis as the reason for prior dupilumab discontinuation, none reported similar events with lebrikizumab (Table ).
